events.title: 27-year-old started a run club to meet new people—now his NYC side hustle brings in $640K a year
events.summary: Life Brides are bringing back the one-night-only bachelorette party Side Hustles NASA engineer spent $200 to start side hustle from closet—it brings in $32K/mo Life I retired early at 40 and spent the last year following BTS around the world—'I feel a sincere sense of gratitude' Startups Abuse survivors nonprofit received $2 million at Olivia Rodrigo's music festival On The Job NYC's 'Baklava Guy' brings in $20K/month selling Turkish pastries At 6 a.m. on Sept. 5, 2025, Owen Akhibi Herrera realized his side hustle was in trouble. Akhibi, the founder of New York City-based social fitness group Peak and Pace, had spent weeks planning a 5K run and after-party on Governor's Island, a former military base off the tip of Manhattan that's only accessible by water. He and his team loaded up 18 trucks with supplies, and planned to put them onto a ferry. The morning before the event, he got a call that the boat broke down, leaving the vehicles stranded on Wall Street in the city's bustling financial district. Worried about refunding 2,000 people who bought tickets to the event, he spent hours on the phone with Governor's Island officials, he says. He managed to get another boat, and the last of his inventory — about 30 port-a-potties — arrived as the first guests got to the island, he adds. By the end of the day, the effort felt worthwhile: Akhibi watched a 25-year-old member place a medal around an older participant's neck at the finish line, he says. Akhibi, 27, originally founded Peak and Pace as a run club in 2024 while working in algorithmic trading sales for investment bank J.P. Morgan. Running with Peak and Pace is always free, and its larger-scale parties typically require a $15 to $25 ticket, he says. Almost entirely through those parties, the company brought in over $640,000 in 2025 revenue, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It. Not every party is profitable, but the company operates overall at a 15% profit margin, says Akhibi, who currently works full-time as the head of partnerships at San Francisco-based AI robotics lab Grounded Superintelligence. He invests the profits back into the side hustle instead of taking a second salary, he says. Run clubs, Akhibi acknowledges, are a dime-a-dozen, with at least 200 in New York alone. Many of them are free to join, and participation grew nearly 60% globally in 2024, the most recent publicly available data on run club participation rates from run tracking app Strava. Gen Z adults, many of whom are at the age where they're moving to new cities for work, particularly seek out social groups like run clubs to make friends and fight loneliness . Akhibi was among those Gen Zers, he says, launching Peak and Pace in July 2024 as a way to create community for himself and others beyond nightlife after moving to New York from London. Entrepreneurial from the start — before Peak and Pace, he had a side hustle selling real estate — he always wanted to monetize his club, so he could bring his community to events that cost money like comedy nights or even ski trips, he says. Using daily social media posts to advertise Peak and Pace, Akhibi grew attendance to roughly 150 runners by its fifth session, after which he hosted a party in a bar in Manhattan that cost about $20 per participant, he says. As participation in the runs grew, so did the parties, featuring DJs and food vendors to justify the ticket cost. Now, Peak and Pace hosts hiking and ski trips outside of the city, too. Gradually, running the club started to feel like a second full-time job, says Akhibi. "I had to keep performing at a very high level in my [day] job. I was put in a place of high responsibility, and so keeping myself in a good mental mindset was probably the hardest thing," he says. Including his side hustle, he worked 18-hour days for about a year, he says. More than 30,000 people ended up attending Peak and Pace events in 2025, Akhibi says, which he took as a sign that running his side hustle on top of his full-time job wouldn't be sustainable for much longer. Somewhat serendipitously for him, he moved to San Francisco in March to accept his current role at Grounded Superintelligence. Peak and Pace now has a team of nine contractors who lead its events almost completely independently from its founder. Akhibi checks in during monthly visits to New York, he says, but is looking for a new head of operations to take over. The lessons he's learned from running Peak and Pace helped him find community in San Francisco, he adds: Making friends means understanding other people, and "working events and dealing with people teaches you [to have] a lot of patience." Patience can especially help you find common ground with other people, Akhibi notes. "Sometimes it can get frustrating when you don't understand somebody's point of view," he says. "If you can just learn to be patient and try to put yourself in their shoes, then you become understanding in almost any given situation.

events.title: OpenAI reveals the AI-era workplace skills that matter most
events.summary: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . OpenAI recently published one of the clearest signals yet about which workplace skills may become most valuable in the AI era. In a report on how its researchers use AI, the company shared data showing which tasks are being absorbed by AI and which still rely on people. The biggest automation gains this year came in coding , technical support, monitoring computer runs, and analyzing results. By contrast, AI is still doing relatively little work deciding what projects to pursue, where to invest resources, or how to set priorities. This offers a glimpse of where the value of work may shift. Companies can measure whether code was written, products shipped, or bugs fixed, making those tasks easier to automate. Deciding what should be built in the first place is harder. It requires judgment, context, tradeoffs, and a willingness to take risks. As OpenAI put it: "People still set our research priorities, judge which ideas and results to pursue, and decide whether to scale, pause, or deploy systems." In other words, the future of human work may shift away from execution and toward making the right decisions. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . events.title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz
events.summary: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms US president Donald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. “They made a proposal but I reject it,” he told reporters at the White House. The US president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal. Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported. Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”. During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would have relieved pressure on global energy markets, and restarting talks on its nuclear programme within seven days. In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”. That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also said to be concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories. Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York. After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.” Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said ⁠late on Saturday that ​Tehran had seen ⁠an initial reaction from ​Trump ‌to ‌its proposal ‌but had yet to receive a response through mediators. Iran ‌was waiting for the mediators ​to convey the definitive US position ⁠and would ​make a ​decision ​based on ​it, he added. Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council. He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said. This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe. Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”. “Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”. Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks. Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy. Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children. Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian. Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict. Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and AP

events.title: Losses at Libya's NOC hit $95m as Zawiya refinery shuts down
events.summary: Libya's National Oil Company has said one of the refineries at its key Zawiya site has been shut down, bringing its financial losses to about $95 million through the week amid fears of wider economic harm. The decision came amid the continued forced closure of Zawiya's valve for its Sharara crude transmission line, spurred by armed groups belonging to the Western South Oil Facilities Guard Agency and Western Military Zone, the state oil company said in a statement on Saturday. That has brought Tripoli-based NOC's lost crude production to more than 942,000 barrels of oil for the week, it said. The losses peaked at nearly 260,000 barrels on Tuesday. NOC "forcibly shut down one of the refining units at the Zawiya refinery to ensure the continued operation of the other unit for as long as possible", it said. Zawiya is Libya’s largest operating refinery, with a refining capacity of 120,000 barrels per day. It produces petrol, diesel, jet fuel, liquefied petroleum gas, fuel oil and naphtha for domestic consumption. The wider site also includes a centre for the production of asphalt and lubricants. The complex is important for the country’s upstream operations because it is connected to Sharara , one of Libya’s largest fields, through a pipeline that transports crude for domestic supply and for export in global markets. The company repeated warnings that the disruption will hit government finances and the overall economy. "The continued disruption of crude oil flow through the main line ... will have a negative impact directly on the country's oil revenues, as well as double the import bill for petroleum products," it said. "Specialised teams ... have programmed a shipment of crude oil through one of the ports to feed the refinery and ensure its continuity of operation, as a precautionary measure to avoid any repercussions that may affect the supplies to electricity generation stations." Libya has been beset with problems, including political instability and violence, after former leader Muammar Qaddafi was overthrown in 2011. Much of its oil production has since remained offline amid unrest. The country is run by two governments, in Tripoli and Benghazi, with the presence of numerous armed groups wielding influence and discouraging investors to pump finances into the country. Libya has the world's 10th-largest proven oil reserves at nearly 48.4 million barrels, which is also the largest in Africa, data from Worldometer shows. Libya needs investment of up to $40 billion to develop its oil and gas sector as it aims to boost production and become a reliable global supplier, NOC chairman Masoud Suleman said last month , while noting "untapped resources". Most of Libya's largest oilfields and export terminals lie in eastern areas controlled by forces commanded by Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, the Financial Times reported in August. In the west, the UN-recognised Government of National Unity is backed by a patchwork of armed groups.

events.title: I quit the corporate job that asked me to do the work of 3 to become an indie game developer who travels the world
events.summary: Kelsey Fiegle Kelsey Fiegle spent seven years as a UX designer until a layoff forced her to take on extra work. After quitting and applying to 100 new jobs, she joined her husband in game development. Fiegle's dress-up game drew millions of plays, and the couple now lives a traveling lifestyle. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kelsey Fiegle, an independent game developer behind Vortella's Dress Up. She developed the game with her husband, Wes Thorburn. Their games are available on the browser gaming platform Poki. The essay has been edited for length and clarity. I spent seven years as a user experience designer at a Chicago creative agency. When two people on my team were laid off , I was expected to take on their work. I remember thinking, "I can't do the work of three people." I left without another job lined up. My husband, Wes Thorburn, who was already developing games independently, thought we could make games together, but I wanted to find another tech role first. After about 100 applications, I decided to give the dress-up game I had been building a real shot, and it changed my life entirely within the month. Client work wore me down Wes and I met in a game design class while I was studying abroad in Australia in 2013. Neither of us was pursuing game design. I took the class because I needed extra credit and thought it sounded fun. After we got married and settled in the US, Wes started experimenting with web games while waiting for his work permit . He eventually released games on Poki, and they began bringing in enough money to help pay our bills. I helped him with sound, 3D modeling, and user experience design while keeping my agency job. For a long time, I was the agency's only UX designer . Some days, I tracked time for 10 different clients. There were weekly presentations, deadlines, and projects that changed when a client mentioned a requirement late in the process. I learned a lot and had a really good team, but the work was stressful. I'd pour my heart into a project, only to find out it was all wrong because the client had forgotten to tell us something. Once, a client needed work finished on short notice. I worked all Saturday and Sunday to get it done. When the client saw it on Monday, they decided they needed a week to review it instead of two days. Moments like that wore me down. A layoff became the last straw Kelsey Fiegle At a game developer conference in 2023, Wes and I asked the Poki team what kinds of games they wanted to see more of. They said dress-up games. I liked making things in 3D, so I began building a 3D dress-up game alongside my full-time job. I had been trying to get more help for my team, so I wouldn't have to work so much. Then the agency laid off two of my coworkers and expected me to pick up their work. I liked my team and didn't want to leave them in a difficult position, so I gave the agency a couple of months to find another solution. But they didn't, so I couldn't keep going. Wes told me, "Kelsey, you can do this. We could do this together. It'd be fine. We could pull this off." I wasn't sure. I was applying hard for jobs because I wanted an in-house tech role , not another agency job. It was difficult to make that move. Going through interviews and getting rejected hurt my confidence , especially when I really wanted a particular job. I told myself that if I reached 100 applications without finding anything, I would try game development. That's what happened. I spent about four months working full time on my dress-up game. I needed income, including money for health insurance , so I eventually released it even though I didn't feel it was finished. "Vortella's Dress Up" launched in December 2024. I was shocked at how well it did. It got about 10 million plays in its first month. The game gave us freedom Vortella's Dressup Poki team members suggested that the game could do even better if it were multiplayer. Until then, Wes and I had mostly worked on separate games. He had experience building multiplayer features for his pizza game, so we decided to develop my game together. Today, the game gets roughly 10 million to 15 million plays a month, though that changes with the season. It has so far reached 276 million total plays from 63.1 million unique players, with 50.6 million hours of total playtime. We keep adding clothing, minigames, and other features, and try to update it at least twice a month. Wes and I had always wanted the flexibility to spend time with his family in Singapore and Australia. We visit them each year and add other destinations when we can. We've traveled to Vietnam and Hong Kong, visited relatives in Italy and Germany, and stopped by Poki's office in Amsterdam. I think about the tech job I wanted so badly during my search. If I were offered it now, I'd turn it down. I have a way better job. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: China wants in on U.S. AI data center boom. Here's why
events.summary: China's AI data center buildout has lagged, and Chinese companies see opportunity in the U.S. market. The U.S. has more AI data centers than any other country and tech giants like Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon keep on funding new projects. Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump spoke about AI this week during Xi's visit to Washington, but geopolitical hurdles remain. China and the U.S. may be competing for dominance in artificial intelligence, but some Chinese manufacturers are eyeing the U.S. data center buildout as an opportunity. "We can see very big potential in the U.S. market," said S.K. Lee, a global vice president with Singapore-registered Brightray, an AI infrastructure company. "The China market is equally important, but we can see that there's a stronger demand in the U.S." Brightray's sole manufacturer is Chinese firm PrefabDC, which makes prefabricated data centers. Brightray manages the construction of the buildouts. Even with public backlash over the AI data center buildout growing, the U.S. boasts more AI data centers than any other country, with 5,427 in 2025, according to data published by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence . China had 449, according to the same report. U.S. tech giants like Alphabet , Microsoft , Meta and Amazon are estimated to spend around $765 billion combined this year on AI infrastructure. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon recently said that figure could hit $1 trillion next year . Chinese companies like Alibaba have committed far less. But the Chinese government has outlined plans to invest $295 billion to build data centers over the next five years, though it's still a far cry from U.S. private-sector investment. "Chinese companies just are not generating as much revenues from their AI services," said Jeffrey Ding, AI expert and assistant professor at The George Washington University. "And that's one of the reasons why they're not able to invest in these enormous data center buildouts that their competitors in the U.S. are doing." Ding said the deeper issue is "there is not as much demand for the AI services." Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington has brought renewed focus on the China-U.S. trade dynamic, and AI was a prominent part of talks between Xi and President Donald Trump . But the relationship between the rivals remains fraught. American policymakers and the security establishment fear cybersecurity risks and worry the U.S. could become reliant on China for critical infrastructure, potentially giving leverage to its main AI competitor. The Trump administration is considering bans on Chinese open-weight AI models as well as new types of Chinese data center components. "It is a very challenging environment between the geopolitics recently between the tariffs we've been seeing and the recent bans," said Benjamin Boucher, principal analyst on supply chains for Wood Mackenzie. "I think it is just going to depend on what we see at a political level over the coming years in terms of how it evolves." Boucher explained that the U.S., which is facing shortages in key components such as electrical equipment, doesn't have a lot of what it needs domestically. And while the U.S. has some components, there are long lead times, and China "can offer those at a much more favorable timing." "China is definitely very important towards the U.S. supply chain for data centers at the moment," Boucher said. China, the world's largest manufacturer, is already deep in the U.S. supply chain and has been for years. Chinese companies supply transformers, batteries and fiber-optic cables, among other products. At a factory in the eastern Chinese trading city of Yangzhou, Brightray's Lee explained how it benefits from China's extensive supply chain. "These materials, equipment are sourced from different parts of the world and a very big portion come from China because China's supply chain is very integrated and comprehensive. That's the reason why we have the factory here in China," Lee said. Prefabricated construction is used in the U.S., but mainly for the modules inside a building rather than modules that include the exterior of the building, as Brightray says it does. The method allows a company to build most of the data center inside a controlled environment to protect against weather and unexpected events at a site. In the U.S., data centers take on average about two to three years to build, industry analysts told CNBC. Brightray said its prefabricated data centers with PrefabDC can cut construction time by at least half. events.title: I paid for a $900 Michelin-star dinner with my son. The price tag was worth it to show him the life he can achieve.
events.summary: The author spent $900 on a fine-dining experience with his adult son. Courtesy of Kimanzi Constable My son was born when I was 19, and we grew up together. I've tried to show him what's possible if he's willing to work for it. I recently took him to a Michelin-star restaurant to show him the life he can have if he succeeds. My first child was born a few days after I turned 19. Looking into his eyes as I held him, I told myself I wanted to give him a better life than I had. I was a homeless teenager , and I had to raise myself. I had to figure everything out and start my adult life from desperation and struggle. I wasn't going to let my son, Michael, experience the same things. I promised myself I would show him a better life and what's possible through my actions. That's why I recently took my adult son to a fine-dining experience in Bangkok. We grew up together, and he got to see my growth By the time he was born, I had started my first business, and it grew quickly. As Michael grew up, he saw the small businesses I started and came to work with me. My son was curious and asked questions about entrepreneurship, money, and what it means to live a good life. We had great conversations on father-son workdays. His mother and I eventually got divorced. I worried it would put emotional distance between us and undo the lessons I was teaching him, but that wasn't the case. We kept building our relationship after the divorce. Michael graduated from high school , went to college, and got an adult job. I was glad to see him applying what I taught him and putting in the work to build his life. I moved outside the US when I became an empty nester After years of traveling and living in a dozen countries, I settled in Bangkok, Thailand . My son recently came to visit me in Thailand, and I wanted to remind him about the conversations we've had about what's possible. Michael came to see his old man, and I took him around the city. I showed him all the touristy things in Bangkok, and he was excited to be on vacation from his job. I took him to a Michelin-star restaurant I've had many fun experiences traveling to 89 countries and have eaten delicious food in many places, but I've never eaten at a Michelin-star restaurant. Michael and I went to Sühring, where I paid $900 for this three-Michelin-star fine-dining experience. The service, the absolutely delicious food, and the time with my oldest child, enjoying the finer things in life, are something I'll never forget. We took our time during the 3.5-hour meal. We savored each course and continued our lifelong conversation about goals, dreams, working hard, and what's possible if you're willing to take action. But the meal was the real conversation: Each course's creativity used taste, texture, presentation, and flavor to create a unique eating experience . I got to try German Whisky for the first time. It was expensive, but sipping it made me feel bougie. Each course and the service gave us an experience we normally don't get. I sat there motivated to work even harder so I could have more experiences like this. I shared that with my son. Even though it was expensive, it was worth every penny to show him the life he can achieve I got to show Micahel he can experience the finer things in life if he's willing to work for them. It made the price worth it. My son saw firsthand that my business's success could let me spend $900 on a meal without thinking about the cost. I didn't get these kinds of experiences growing up, and it affected my mindset negatively. I started my adult life with so many limiting beliefs because I didn't have anyone to show me otherwise. Thank goodness for therapy, which helped me overcome my past trauma and learn to see what's possible for my life. I'm grateful for this Michelin-star experience, despite the price. My son left Thailand with a vivid life lesson in the best way possible. I feel I'm doing my part as a father to raise a strong young man. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: U.S. and China agree to "super intelligence" dialogue amid AI tensions
events.summary: The U.S. and China have agreed to set up a dialogue on artificial intelligence , with a communications channel to help defuse serious incidents, the White House said overnight. Why it matters: President Trump has said the main thing that matters in the AI race is beating China — but the pact acknowledges that they're serious competition, too. Driving the news: The White House released a fact sheet late Friday night with outcomes from Trump's summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The two sides agreed to refer to AI as "super intelligence" or "SI," the White House said — Trump's new and preferred term for the technology. They will create a "U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue" to meet on "risks and benefits related to SI," with the next meeting by November. Zoom in: The administration also said there would be a "bilateral communication channel for SI incidents," which some have likened to a Cold War-era " red telephone " between the two nations. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent focused on creating the channel during last weekend's pre-summit meetings with Chinese officials. Yes, but: It's not clear what kind of incidents would rise to the level of using the channel, or what kinds of notifications each side would give the other.

events.title: UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against Palestinians
events.summary: Israel ‘categorically rejects’ publication and says businesses on database have committed no wrongdoing The UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it says are involved in violating Palestinian human rights through business ties to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank . The vast majority of the total 214 companies, which are based in 11 countries, are Israeli. Five of the 158 companies listed last year were removed in the latest update. The blacklist, first published in 2020, was born of a vote by the UN’s human rights council, which has no ability to force companies to act. Its main goal is to name and shame businesses with ties to the settlements. It is unclear how the inclusion on the list has affected the companies financially. “This report is another reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities and are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses,” said Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, in a statement. Israel said it “categorically rejects” the publication. “This database is meant to serve as a blacklist against businesses that have committed no wrongdoing,” the Israeli diplomatic mission in Geneva said in a statement. “We call on friends not to yield to this ugly attempt to blacklist Israeli firms.” The UN office said it had advised the companies of their listing and given them a right of reply. The latest report comes as Israeli settlements in Palestinian areas have faced new scrutiny. Earlier this month, Britain banned trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, where it says “settler terrorists” are carrying out “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians. France and Canada announced they would take similar action.

events.title: I'm 72 and don't want to move to a retirement home. So I built a tiny home in my yard for a future live-in caretaker.
events.summary: Jerry and Kathie Schwartz. Courtesy of Kathie Schwartz. In their 70s, Kathie Schwartz and her husband found their three-story home difficult to navigate. They moved into a smaller one-story home and built a 480-square-foot tiny home in the backyard. The tiny home will eventually house a live-in caretaker, allowing them to age in place. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kathie Schwartz, 72, who built a tiny home in her California backyard. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I wanted to get ahead of planning for old age . My husband and I are in our 70s and in very good health, but we've been losing friends and going to a lot of celebrations of life. At our age, that's pretty common. After one celebration of life, my husband looked at me and said, "Promise me you'll never put me in a home." That was kind of my jumping-off point: What were our options? I started thinking about whether our home was still right for us and whether we were living in the right place. I had gone through it with my parents and watched friends go through it, too. At the time, we were living in a three-story, 3,600-square-foot home in Truckee, California, near Lake Tahoe . In the winter, we could get 22 feet of snow in our yard. There was one year we didn't see our front door for three months. At a certain age, there's a limit to how long you can live in that kind of snow. We decided it was best to downsize and move , especially as many of our friends were leaving the area. We don't want to live in a retirement community At first, we considered living in a retirement community. We visited places all over — Nevada, Central California, and other areas where older people go for low taxes and to have a resort-style lifestyle. I'll tell you, while these places have everything you could need, there's just something weird about them. One of the places we tried out was a beautiful development in Arizona. It was in the middle of nowhere. You drive through nothing, and then all of a sudden, the gates open, and there are waterfalls, palm trees, stadium pickleball courts, mahjong rooms, and golf courses. They had beautiful model homes lined up on a block. You could pick everything, from the furnishings to the lot you wanted, and they would just plop the whole thing down for you. We stayed there for two or three days. As we were leaving, the gate opened, and beyond it was just the desert. My husband stopped the car at the gate, looked at me, and said, "There is no way I'm ever living here." I said, "I hear you." That crossed it off the list. First, we downsized to a much smaller home We eventually decided to move into a home we owned in Petaluma, California. It's a single-story, 1,100-square-foot house built in 1924. We'd bought it 35 years earlier and had always used it as a rental property. It was quite a shock to go from our 3,600-square-foot Truckee home to 1,100 square feet. But this little home is worth well over $1 million. If we wanted a place with extra bedrooms or guest rooms, we'd be looking at close to $2 million just to get something comparable to our old home. The house has a backyard, but it wasn't much of one. For a while, I kept thinking, "Okay, what would I put back there? How could we use it?" Around that time, a friend of mine who lives with her mother bought a large piece of property. Her mother still wanted to maintain her independence, so she built her a tiny home in the backyard. While my friend was researching and planning the construction, we talked about it all the time. It inspired me to build one of our own, though it took a while to convince my husband. Then we built a tiny home in our backyard We decided to build with Colorado-based Studio Home. For about a year, I played around on their website, designing what I envisioned. Eventually, we hired a landscape architect and decided to build a 480-square-foot unit, the largest we could on the property. The permitting process took about a year before we could begin construction. And then, of course, there were so many decisions to make: what kind of windows we wanted, what finishes to use — it was a lot. The Schwartz tiny home was built by Colorado-based Studio Home. Courtesy of Kathie Schwartz Once construction started, though, it went pretty quickly. The foundation took the longest, along with trenching for the sewer and electrical lines. We completed building in 2022. The home has a kitchen and a bathroom, and instead of building a separate bedroom, I put in a Murphy bed. In all, the project cost about $280,000. Adding this tiny home to our property was truly one of the best real-estate decisions I've ever made. Not only did it increase the value of our property, but it has also given us so much flexibility. We plan to age in place here We use our tiny home for many things. First, it serves as a guest house when people come through town, since our main house is too small to comfortably host guests. Living in Petaluma is expensive, so building the tiny home was a more practical option than trying to find a larger house. Second, I teach mahjong , so I host classes there. And third, our longer-term goal is that, if I eventually need to hire someone to help care for us — as we don't have children — they could live in the tiny home. That way, we wouldn't have to move to a retirement community, which can be very expensive. The Murphy bed and kitchen. Courtesy of Kathie Schwartz The goal is always to stay in our home as long as possible. By building this tiny house , we have so many more options depending on my health. It's given us so much freedom. I have this conversation with my friends all the time. We don't have to go the route our parents went, right? We're a different generation; we don't need to end up in a retirement home. We've decided to band together and plan for our futures. We've talked about buying a larger piece of property and putting a bunch of tiny homes on it so we can live together as a community. As you get older, you want to live somewhere you're comfortable and be around the people you care about. Sometimes the people you consider family aren't necessarily your birth family — your friends become your community and support system. Read the original article on Business Insider

As laid out by the White House, it would also potentially lower prices on a variety of consumer goods where American shoppers have felt the pinch of inflation. Between the lines: The White House also said China would import 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and again in 2028. The country was a top-five importer of U.S. coal until slashing imports in 2025 amid the trade war. The intrigue: The fact sheet released by the White House was more vague on the fate of the crucial rare earth minerals that have been at the heart of the trade dispute. "The United States and China continue to work on U.S. concerns regarding supply chain shortages related to rare earths and other critical minerals, with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels," it said,.

events.title: Work intensifying on UK laws to stamp out concert ticket touts, say sources
events.summary: Artists including Tinie Tempah and the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce ramp up pressure on government to keep its pledge to outlaw for-profit resales The government has stepped up work on new laws to stop ticket touts fleecing fans , as the prime minister came under pressure from artists including the drummer from the Smiths, one of his favourite bands. Keir Starmer said last year that the government would “stop fans from being ripped off” by outlawing the for-profit resale of tickets on sites such as Viagogo and StubHub, a pledge Labour first made in its 2024 election manifesto. Despite support from a host of globally renowned artists, including Radiohead, Dua Lipa and Coldplay, the measure was not included in this year’s king’s speech , prompting concern among music industry figures that the proposal had been shelved. But multiple sources told the Guardian that the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) has assembled a sizeable “bill team”, a group of civil servants who are drafting the policy and will help shepherd it through parliament. They are understood to be considering ways to mitigate the risk that touts and resale platforms simply base themselves offshore to bypass any new legislation. The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, told the House of Commons this month that Andy Burnham “feels particularly passionate” about the issue and the government would treat it as a priority. Nandy is due to give a speech at Labour conference on Wednesday, at which she could provide further detail. On Friday, industry figures and artists including the rapper Tinie Tempah and the Smiths’ drummer Mike Joyce called on the prime minister to act fast, citing new evidence of touts targeting small venues in Greater Manchester. Research examined 300 events across 13 venues where tickets were being touted on Viagogo , including Band On The Wall, Gorilla, YES, Rebellion, New Century and the White Hotel. All were advertised at significantly over cost price, while some did not feature information about the seller, an apparent breach of competition rules. Under government plans, companies would face much tougher penalties for failing to enforce these rules. Other tickets appeared to be “speculative”, meaning that they had been fraudulently listed by touts who do not have them but hope to procure some once they have agreed a sale. The most expensive was £5,899 for Mica Millar’s show at New Century – a 19,728% mark-up. Tickets to a 40th anniversary celebration of the Smiths’ The Queen Is Dead, featuring a conversation between Joyce and the producer Stephen Street, were being touted for £549 each. Joyce said it was “time to stop this for good”, while Tempah said fans and artists deserved better than to see tickets “siphoned away by people who contribute nothing to live music but are happy to profit from it”. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Just three touts – based in Latvia, North America and Germany – were responsible for more than 75% of the listings, research by the music industry group FanFair Alliance found. Viagogo dispute the claim, saying the proportion held by the trio was significantly lower. Viagogo also listed tickets for tiny, obscure events, including an evening with the “world’s greatest psychic” in Inverness, a rum tasting in Devizes, and stargazing in Tavistock. The company said actual sale prices were much lower than the high-priced listings identified by FanFair Alliance. “Viagogo takes its obligations under the law seriously and is fully compliant in the UK. Our policies prohibit speculative listings,” it added. If the government does go ahead with a ban on ticket touting, it would bring the UK in line with Ireland, which outlawed touting in 2021. At present, the unauthorised resale of football tickets is illegal across the UK. Resale of concert or theatre tickets without authorisation is permitted, although individual touts have been prosecuted and jailed in rare instances where they have been judged to have committed fraud. Fans lost £60m to touts between Labour’s announcement of the policy and April this year, the telecoms company and venue sponsor O2 has estimated, with fans of acts including Olivia Dean, Bad Bunny and Ariana Grande “fleeced” by markups of up to 1,000%. The Guardian has repeatedly exposed exploitative tactics in secondary ticketing, including speculative selling and the use by touts of specialist software to hoover up tickets and flip them for profit, often via sites such as StubHub and Viagogo. A DCMS spokesperson said: “We are fully committed to stamping out ticket touting for good. For too long, fans have been ripped off and we’re determined to right that wrong. “That’s why we are bringing forward draft legislation in this parliamentary session to ensure that our measures are truly effective, enforceable and future-proof and fans get the protection and security they have always deserved.”

events.title: ‘It’s just getting worse’: anger in Maine over Trump’s trade war with close neighbor Canada
events.summary: President’s tariffs have hurt fishers, loggers and others in a state with deep bonds to Canada – will voters show their displeasure in the midterms? It was an ideal summer to cut trees. The weather in Maine’s Penobscot county – one of the most heavily forested counties in a state dense with trees – was warm and dry. Yet even as the county’s wood had grown to an ideal size to harvest, the machines Molly London typically uses sat idle. London and her husband, Alex, who started a logging business nearly 10 years ago, had been waiting weeks for replacement machine parts that were no longer stocked locally because tariffs had made them too expensive. By August, she and her husband decided to shut down their business, WW London Woodlot Management Company, exhausted after years of fighting ever-climbing costs. “It just didn’t feel right any more,” she said. “We’ve been losing for a long time, and this is just getting worse.” For centuries, Maine’s economy has been inextricably tied to logging. Penobscot styled itself the “lumber capital of the world” in the 19th century, and today, hulking timber lorries still take up half of the road when they charge down Maine’s rural interstates. The aroma from spruce and fir trees can be smelled through a closed car window. Logging’s health is a crucial bellwether for the overall state of its economy, and things are looking bleak in the midst of a trade war with Canada and record-high diesel prices. Democrats are hoping the frustration will finally unseat Republican Susan Collins, whose loss is crucial in helping the party win a majority in the US Senate. But after the fallout of Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race in July amid sexual assault allegations, the party has been scrambling to make up for lost time. In his first campaign ad, Troy Jackson – formerly the state’s senate president who lost a bid to be the state’s governor earlier this year – immediately labeled himself as a “fifth-generation logger”. “Susan Collins is just a rubber-stamp for the wealthy elite in this country,” Jackson said in another campaign ad. Sara Gideon, a former state representative, had run similar attack ads in 2020, telling voters that Collins is “Not For You Anymore” – an attempt to tie her to Trump and the wealthy elite. It didn’t work. Though the state voted for Joe Biden, it re-elected Collins at the same time, though no public polls had showed her with a lead in the race. This election, Collins continues to highlight that she is a girl from Caribou who hails from a lumber family. Her seniority in the Senate has also given her power: Collins has been a senator for 29 years, making her the fifth longest-serving senator, and is the chair of the Senate’s powerful appropriations committee. “I am a county girl,” Collins said, while sat on a pile of potatoes for a recent campaign ad featuring Mainers saying the senator is “just like us”. The state, with a population of 1.4 million people, leans Democrat, driven by strong liberal support along its coast, and has not voted for a Republican president since George HW Bush in 1988. Unlike their more liberal counterparts down south, Mainers pride themselves on having a more independent streak. While it’s still unclear how voters in the state will turn out in the midterms – Collins and Jackson are currently neck-and-neck in the polls – some voters have been feeling left behind. “It feels like the things that were promised to get into office now don’t come through,” London said. “I think this area is definitely feeling the impact of that.” Maine’s economy is deeply intertwined with Canada, sending roughly 40% of its exports to its northern neighbor, according to the Maine International Trade Center. But their relationship goes far beyond trade. This is a state where Canadian and American flags can be seen flying side by side, where entire towns cater specifically to Canadian tourists. “There are generational bonds. We share our largest border with Canada. A lot of Mainers can trace their history through Canada,” said Patrick Woodcock, the president of the Maine State Chamber of Commerce. “There’s a business relationship as well, but also familial. … We have a little bit of a shared destiny together.” That relationship has been sorely tested by the breakdown in relations by Trump’s trade war. After negotiations between the two countries broke down at the 11th hour, Trump announced a 50% tariff on select Canadian goods that began 22 August. In response, Canada introduced its own retaliatory tariffs, ranging from 15% to 50%, targeting $20bn worth of American imports with levies that took effect earlier this month. For Maine loggers, this means many of the parts and equipment they usually buy from Canada and other countries have been hit by tariffs, said Dana Doran, the executive director of the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast.

events.title: London transfer: is it time to kill off the Heathrow Express?
events.summary: With fares high and passenger numbers low, plans for a third runway could bring the train’s future into question I f Heathrow finally builds its third runway, Londoners can expect hundreds more planes flying overhead each day. But greater congestion on the ground will be a problem too. Under Heathrow’s £33bn expansion plan , 100,000-200,000 more passengers would eventually be travelling to or from the airport each day. The most eye-catching problem has been moving part of the UK’s busiest motorway, the M25, to make space for a new 2.2-mile (3.5km) runway. A thornier one may be getting motorists out of their cars, and finding more sustainable ways for the extra passengers – and thousands of staff – to travel to and from Heathrow. Although ride-sharing, coaches and buses can play a part, scaling up rail is the clear alternative. Space on the existing line is, however, at a premium, and the Elizabeth line, built with a promise of connecting business travellers swiftly and directly from Heathrow to the City and Canary Wharf, only has limited paths. With everything up for negotiation, transport experts are asking: has the time come to kill off the Heathrow Express? The obvious airport train, as unwary visitors often find out too late, may not be the best one. The Heathrow Express, which charges a whopping £26 for a 15- to 21-minute one-way hop, was long one of the most expensive airport connections around (at least until it was overtaken by the Luton Dart ). It is, as advertised, technically the fastest way to central London, though passengers travelling beyond Paddington may reach their destination more quickly on the Elizabeth line or even the tube on a direct route. For those who value the speed – in addition to TV news, a toilet and a luggage rack – it may be the perfect service. But the Heathrow Express was only used by 4.5 million passengers last year, a figure that represents, at best, less than 6% of Heathrow’s air passengers, with the number bolstered by airport staff on heavily discounted tickets. Transport for London (TfL) has signalled its belief that the service’s time is up, as the government consults on its Heathrow expansion national policy statement. MPs must approve the statement for the runway to go ahead. That no longer seems automatic: Andy Burnham’s long-term scepticism over a third runway, along with the loss of Rachel Reeves in No 11 as a champion of expansion, makes Downing Street support look ambivalent at best – even given the new chancellor’s belated assertion that the “economic case stacks up”. The Sunday Times reported this weekend that airport bosses have told ministers the third runway will not now be operational until 2039, a four year delay. However many runways the airport has, TfL said it was “worth reviewing [the Heathrow Express’s] future in the context of determining the optimal mix of services on the Great Western mainline to make the most effective use of the limited capacity available”. For TfL, the Elizabeth line, going deeper and cheaper into the heart of London , is “a more compelling service”. At the moment, only two Elizabeth line trains an hour serve Heathrow’s Terminal 5, which handles about 40% of the airport’s passengers. That means a passenger who does not carefully judge the timing may face a journey from the City or Canary Wharf to T5 of more than an hour. The frequency is due to double next year but more space into Heathrow could still be freed up. Alex Williams, the chief customer and strategy officer at TfL, told MPs at a select committee hearing this month that the Heathrow Express was “taking up valuable paths that aren’t actually well used. There’s a way of repurposing that to be more affordable, more attractive, and carry more public transport users.” Surface access, or getting people between central London and Britain’s biggest airport, underwent a step change with the Elizabeth line. Previously, the little-advertised offering Heathrow Connect joined the dots at the likes of Hayes & Harlington on a slower train to Paddington, serving many airport workers, if not international travellers. Fares were then about a third of the price of the Heathrow Express – a gap that is now less significant given that the Elizabeth line charges £15.50 to reach any of its central London stations. And for those who are able to book and plan a month ahead, the Express advance tickets can prove less expensive at £10. TfL’s cheaper but slower alternative, the Piccadilly line (£5.90 into central London), is also due to get an upgrade of signalling and trains, increasing capacity. Two additional rail schemes have been mooted – Heathrow Southern Railway and a Western Rail link – as ways to connect into the wider national rail network, and the Elizabeth line itself could be extended to Staines – all of which would encourage many more from the suburban commuter belt to take the train rather than drive to the airport.

events.title: I'm approaching 40 with no real retirement plan. My wife and I have accepted that I'll just keep working.
events.summary: The author (not pictured) has realized that 'soft retirement' is probably in his future. Delmaine Donson/Getty Images Every year, my wife and I have the same conversation about retirement. Another thing that happens every year? We realize that it's likely not doable. However, I'm OK with 'soft retirement.' Working gives me purpose. I turn 40 in a few months. Every year around my birthday, my wife and I have the same conversation. We make coffee, the kids disappear into a screen for an hour, and we pull up the numbers. Between our day jobs and my freelance writing side hustle , we earn enough to pay our mortgage, save a bit, and provide our kids with everything they need. On paper, we're fine. What we don't have is what many people in our parents' generation had and worked toward: a date on the calendar when work stops, and retirement begins . We keep running the numbers and landing in the same place We've run the numbers with various spreadsheets and different assumptions, but always land at the same conclusion: There's no realistic version where I stop working at 60 or 65 and coast on savings for a few decades. The honest projection is that I'll probably still be writing and working for myself in some form or another at 70 and beyond. At first, this idea scared me. It felt like failure, like I'd missed a milestone everyone else was striving for. Both my parents retired with pensions and celebrations, so it's been ingrained in me that you work hard for 30 years, then kick back and relax. But I don't buy it. Planning around an ending I don't believe in Traditional retirement planning assumes a cliff. You work, and then one day you don't, and everything after that is the reward. My wife and I have slowly stopped believing in the cliff. Not just because we don't think we'll be able to afford it, but also because I've realized I don't want it. I like working. It gives me purpose. I'd be restless and depressed within a month without it. So our annual conversation has changed. It used to be 'How do we get to the finish line?" Now it's, "If we have no finish line, what do we want the next few decades to feel like?" The part I can't put in a spreadsheet There's a variable that no projection accounts for: whether my work will still exist in 20 to 30 years. I write for a living, and I'd be lying if I said the rise of AI wasn't nestled in the back of my mind every time we open that spreadsheet. It's challenging to plan to write at 70 when I can't say for certain that the industry will need a human writer at 50. That uncertainty is newer than the retirement question, and in some ways it's scarier, because I may not even have the option to write for a living. I can't control the wave, so my only real move is to get good at riding it. I've started folding AI into my own workflow, using it to research faster and handle the grunt work, so the part that's truly me, the judgment and the voice, is where I spend my time. Maybe that keeps me employable longer. Maybe it doesn't. What we've landed on instead The idea that intrigues me most is what people are starting to call soft retirement . Not stopping working altogether, but scaling back as I age and our finances are more secure. It's the only version of the future that feels both realistic and good. I don't need to grind at this pace forever. But the plan where I keep writing a couple of days a week into my 70s on projects I choose, while doing more of the things I actually moved to a small town for, that one I can get behind. events.title: Adnoc's XRG prepares for next phase of Azerbaijan gas development
events.summary: XRG, Adnoc's international energy investment unit , is to boost its gas portfolio with plans for the next phase of its strategic field development in Azerbaijan. The final investment decision for the Absheron offshore gas and condensate field development, where XRG holds a 30 per cent stake, was made alongside Azerbaijan's state oil company Socar and France's TotalEnergies, XRG said in a statement on Saturday. XRG's acquisition of the stake was first announced in 2023 . Socar and TotalEnergies each have a 35 per cent holding in the venture. The XRG announcement was made during the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in the capital Baku. The company did not disclose the value of investments involved. The Caspian Sea field, where production is projected to begin in 2029, is expected to produce up to 600 million cubic feet (17 million cubic metres) of gas and 47,000 barrels of condensate a day, it said. Recoverable gas resources at Absheron are pegged at up to five trillion cubic feet. Mohamed Al Aryani, president of XRG's international gas unit, said Azerbaijan had been able to boost its position as a "critical bridge" between Caspian resources and international markets. "The decision marks an important step forward for XRG and reinforces Azerbaijan's role as a trusted energy partner to international markets," he said. "We are investing in world-class resources and infrastructure that support energy security, create economic value and drive long-term growth." XRG has been actively increasing its portfolio of investments globally and plans to double its asset value over the next decade. Launched in 2024 as an international lower-carbon energy and chemicals investment company, with an enterprise value exceeding $80 billion, it has acquired stakes in several global gas projects. XRG, along with Adnoc and Masdar, this month announced agreements with German companies covering liquefied natural gas, renewable energy, advanced materials and technology. Last month, XRG entered Venezuela's energy sector through an offshore natural gas project alongside global oil company BP and Qatar’s UCC Holding. In June, XRG and Italy's Eni signed agreements with Argentina’s YPF to acquire stakes in three upstream blocks to supply a new LNG project in the South American nation. In January, XRG said it increased its stake in ​the Rio Grande LNG project in the US by 7.6 per cent to build its portfolio . Azerbaijan, meanwhile, has the world's 20th-biggest gas reserves at nearly 1.7 trillion cubic metres, which is less than one per cent of the global total, data compiled by Worldometer shows. Energy products comprise nearly 90 per cent of Azerbaijan’s total exports. Italy is its top export destination, with its other top trading partners including Germany, India and the UK. Azerbaijan’s oil and gas sector offers a solid foundation for expansion into downstream petrochemicals and advanced materials, including refined petroleum products, polymers and specialty chemicals. The country's geographical position – between the Caspian Sea, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe – enables the development of a full-service energy trading hub, analysts at consultancy Oliver Wyman said. Investments in infrastructure, including roads, railways, water supply systems, electricity networks, schools, hospitals and irrigation, have also helped modernise the country's physical capital, the World Bank said. "Through its investments in Absheron, the Southern Gas Corridor and wider Caspian opportunities, XRG is building a long-term platform for growth that supports Azerbaijan's energy ambitions while strengthening regional energy security and advancing its international gas growth strategy," XRG said.

events.title: Got a scratchy throat and runny nose? BI's health team shared their tips for staying healthy.
events.summary: Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Are you sick too? "Anyone else not feeling well?" That was a Monday morning text from one of my closest friends after we had spent a weekend with our crew to close out the summer. And you know what? Yup, we were all feeling a little tickle in our throats. It didn't stop there; I saw more masks during my workday commute and even noticed a few extra sneezes in our newsroom. After doing my own unscientific research, I was calling it: We're all feeling a bit sick . Whether it was the sudden drop in temperatures here in the Tri-State area, seasonal allergies kicking up, or back-to-school sniffles, it seems like a lot of people need their immune systems to kick into high gear. So I asked Business Insider's health team for advice on how to stay healthy during this time of year, notorious for extra germs. Mia de Graaf, executive editor : "Sleep is the Honda Civic of staying healthy: reliable, effective, just not sexy. While everyone is cold-plunge-obsessed, I'm catching Zs (or trying to, when my infant daughter isn't keeping me up). Sleep is when your immune system trains and deploys cells to fight off viruses. Skimp on it, and you're essentially showing up to flu season with a short-handed defense." Hilary Brueck, correspondent : "When it's cold season, I endorse one essential mineral: zinc . It's the only supplement studies have reliably and consistently shown can shorten the duration of a common cold by about a day or two. I usually drink mine with powders like EmergenC and Airborne in my cupboard. Just don't overdo it, as getting too much of this antiviral compound blocks the absorption of other nutrients. 8-10 mg is a good baseline." Kashmira Gander, senior editor : "I try to get my nutrients from food instead of supplements. That changes in the fall when it's difficult to absorb vitamin D from the sun in gloomy London, where I live. As a kid, my mom would give me a spoonful of cod liver oil each morning, but now I prefer it in pill form (because, obviously, gross). Whatever your preferred source, vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and phosphorus from food, and supports the immune system." Gabby Landsverk, correspondent : "My go-to when I can't afford to get sick, especially when I'm competing during roller derby seasons, is a homemade potion. It's a combo of lemon juice and honey with turmeric, black pepper, and cayenne — all of which have some solid science on supporting the immune system and reducing inflammation — mixed with hot water for a soothing boost." events.title: Wall Street week ahead: consumer confidence, inflation, employment updates
events.summary: Wall Street has a busy week ahead with important updates on inflation, the jobs market and consumer confidence NEW YORK -- Wall Street has a busy week ahead with important updates on inflation, the jobs market and consumer confidence. The reports could help provide a clearer picture on how consumers are handling higher prices on a wide range of products and services, along with whether employment and wages remain resilient. Business group The Conference Board will release its consumer confidence survey for September on Tuesday. The survey has revealed shaky confidence from consumers throughout the year. In August, confidence slipped to its lowest level in seven months. On Wednesday, the U.S. will release a key inflation report, the personal consumption expenditures price index, for August. The PCE is closely monitored by Wall Street and the Federal Reserve. Inflation remains stubbornly above 3% and the Federal Reserve recently raised interest rates in an effort to tame high prices. The central bank has a target rate for inflation of 2%. Iran live updates: Trump rejects Iran offer to reopen Strait of Hormuz Trump-Xi takeaways: White House touts progress on AI, Iran and exports Strait of Hormuz shut until Tehran's conditions met, Ghalibaf says High gasoline prices have been fueling a broader jump in inflation, squeezing household budgets and sapping consumer confidence. The U.S. war with Iran has stifled global oil supplies since late February. It has a direct impact via higher gasoline prices, but higher fuel costs also make shipping more expensive. That raises prices for everything from food to clothing. The U.S. releases its monthly employment report for September on Friday. The jobs market has been among the more resilient areas of the economy, but it has started to show more signs of stress. Wage growth has been slowing, which makes it harder for workers to deal with the impact of rising inflation. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Your spare Android won’t come back to life in a hurry but – like neglected PCs – it really should Space Jam: UK debuts space squadron to protect satellites 20 hours ago Valen creator drives 'Golden Spike' to connect new languages with Rust 1 day ago Microsoft cells out, crams multiple values into Excel boxes 1 day ago Uncle Sam coughs up $1.9B for grid upgrades as datacenters hit a power wall 1 day ago Fake Google Security Team ad says 'no script reading' in voice phishing - then prints the script 1 day ago Our resident Microsoft-watcher Richard Speed last week wrote about his seven-hour odyssey bringing a Windows 11 box up to snuff with the latest patches. I’ll see you that struggle, Richard, and raise you my experience updating a 2022-vintage Samsung Galaxy A33 Android smartphone. I spent about a year using the A33 as my daily driver and while it always did a job, the midrange machine is far from the speediest of smartphones and therefore a little frustrating to use. When a great deal for a premium handset came along I splashed some cash and shelved the A33 as a spare, safe in the knowledge that Samsung has promised to support it with new security updates until 2027. I store the A33 in the Basket Full Of Old Tech I Should Probably Have Thrown Out But Kept Just In Case , which sits on the floor of my home office – a room that gets no direct sunlight but is small, warm, and dry. All through the mild-if-clammy winter here in The Register ’s Sydney, Australia, eyrie, the phone insisted it had moisture in its USB-C port and refused to charge. Because it’s a budget model, topping it up with wireless power isn’t an option. Spring has since sprung, so when the mercury topped 30°C (86°F) last weekend I left the phone in a warm and breezy spot for an afternoon. The phantom moisture evaporated, and before long I had the phone charged and running. Within seconds it suggested installing an OS update from April 2025, followed by six more – each of which required manual consent for download and install. The A33’s sluggishness soon manifested as an overlapping mess of updates in progress and reboots to finish installation of the last update. Every few minutes, the phone wanted me to approve or schedule a new download, or log back in. The phone is not so important to me that I needed to get all the updates installed ASAP. Two days of occasional attention at mealtimes and bedtime earned me a slow, old, but functional backup phone. My experience led me to concur with Mr Speed’s excellent argument that vendors need to ship better software so they’re less reliant on updates – and improve the process of updating devices. For Samsung that means rolling up past updates into cumulative downloads so leaving a device offline for a few months requires one intervention to modernize a device. The Korean giant could also do well to detect when a handset needs multiple updates and then inform users that its Smart Switch desktop app makes it possible to install cumulative updates in one fell swoop.

events.title: The customer isn't always right. At least according to Lufthansa's viral complaint clapback.
events.summary: Lufthansa apologized to a customer on X after sarcastically responding to their complaint. Joan Valls/Urbanandsport/NurPhoto via Getty Images Lufthansa's sarcastic reply to a customer got more than 15 million views before it apologized. While other airlines mock passengers to boost PR, that doesn't work for everyone. The rise of AI is complicating customer service, but experts said finding a solution matters most. Does the customer always have to be right? Germany's national airline has apologized after its snarky reply went viral this week, raising important points about customer relations and brand strategy. After an X user accused Lufthansa of ignoring their messages about a payment issue, the airline appeared fed up as it issued a sardonic reply on Tuesday. "We've already responded to you numerous times via DM on different social media platforms," they said. "The response isn't going to magically change just because you're asking the same question on X now." While Ryanair, the Irish budget airline, has built a reputation for mocking its passengers on social media, that's not a germane strategy for everyone. "The way an airline responds to customers online also has to be authentic to its established tone and personality," said Marc Cornelius, the founder and CEO of 8020 Communications, a PR firm specializing in aviation and travel. "You might almost expect a provocative or cheeky response from Ryanair , because it has spent years cultivating that persona, but from Lufthansa it feels out of character and therefore jars." We’ve already responded to you numerous times via DM on different social media platforms. The response isn’t going to magically change just because you’re asking the same question on X now. /Flo — Lufthansa (@lufthansa) September 22, 2026 Some social media users loved it, though. Lufthansa's reply got over 15 million views and 30,000 likes within two days. It was re-shared by meme accounts with millions of followers. However, the airline backtracked within 24 hours, just as the post was picking up steam. "We sincerely apologize for our last reply to you," it said. "This is not the way we treat our passengers." The customer said they appreciated the apology but were still annoyed that their payment dilemma hadn't been resolved and their emails remained unanswered. Lufthansa did not respond to a request for comment. "I feel for the CMO and larger support team at Lufthansa right now. Customers can be demanding, but they're why we exist," Latané Conant, chief marketing officer at AI customer service company Parloa, told Business Insider. The rise of AI is making customer service a more pertinent issue. On the one hand, agents and chatbots make it easier for customers to send detailed complaints and follow up repeatedly. Meanwhile, more companies are using AI to answer them — adding to the pressure on humans doing the same job. While Lufthansa hasn't said whether AI played a role in the incident, Conant said, "It appears to be either a poorly built AI agent or a human badly in need of a vacation." "Which is unfortunate, because either way, it's entirely preventable," she added. People are divided on how helpful AI is for customer service . Ada, an AI customer service firm, commissioned a survey of 1,000 Americans in April and found that half of travelers don't mind if they're answered by an AI or human agent — so long as their problem is resolved. So even as the world of customer service is changing, one thing remains constant: finding a solution. "When a company does get it wrong, a quick and sincere apology is usually the right response," Cornelius told Business Insider. Conant also said that "the immediate apology was 100% the right move, even if it may already be too late." However, Cornelius added, that isn't the be-all and end-all: "The customer needs to feel they've genuinely been heard and, crucially, that the underlying issue is followed up and resolved promptly." events.title: Could an iced coffee freeze you out of the job market?
events.summary: Watch: Is it OK to take an iced coffee to a job interview? Would you bring an iced coffee to a job interview? The question on the internet's lips this week started life, as many do, in a TikTok video. "Don't waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee, it just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand," said US recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen. It's what her Gen Z job candidates are doing, she said, warning it makes it look like the interview is "just a stop on your list of errands for the day". The post has started what Wehniainen calls the Great Iced Coffee Debate of 2026. Some believe turning up with an iced matcha latte in hand is a cardinal sin. They say it's unprofessional, too informal, and a distraction. Others feel this is an overreaction - distracting from how difficult it is to secure a job - or even just get an interview in the first place. In a subsequent LinkedIn post, Wehniainen says she "was never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate. "My point was simply about avoiding distractions." Can an iced latte actually hurt your chances of getting a job? Hanad, 28, works for an energy supplier in London. He likes iced coffee but wouldn't bring one to an interview. "A job interview is all about first impressions," he says. "Anything can deter the employer from employing you. "Iced coffee is something a lot of teens drink… it would look immature and too informal." Hanad says he wouldn't take an iced coffee to an interview He would never bring along an energy drink for the same reasons. But he says water or a hot coffee would be okay. His colleague Tsvetina, 24, thinks a potential employee shouldn't be judged by what they bring to the interview, nor their dress code. "I think we should be moving away from these traditional corporate stigmas. What matters is what the person is actually communicating during the interview." Aisha, 28, says she would take along an iced coffee. "I think it shows that I have come early enough to get iced coffee." She wouldn't bring a fizzy drink, however. In general, she thinks a lot of employers like to see personality in a candidate. "It makes you stand out from other people who are coming [applying] for the job." Katy feels there is a sexist element to the controversy around Wehniainen's post Katy, 25, a personal assistant in events, says she personally wouldn't turn up to a job interview with an iced coffee. But she sees the controversy around Wehniainen's post as "a bit sexist, because it's usually girls who drink iced coffee". "If it was a hot coffee, which is more masculine, there wouldn't be a discourse about that." Young people trying to land their first job are facing multiple challenges. The number of graduate vacancies in the UK has almost halved in the past year , as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs. Around one in eight people aged 16-24 are not in education, employment or training - so called Neets. Young workers in the US are also struggling with a tight jobs market , external as hiring slows. Lucy Cooper is the founder of Spark, a design and branding recruitment company in London. She says her industry - marketing - is really tough right now, and she doesn't know of any Gen Z candidates who would risk turning up to an interview with an iced coffee. You could "seem too relaxed and a little bit flippant, like you're not taking it seriously enough, or you are interviewing the employer rather than the other way round". "I think people at junior level are very conscious about not doing anything that could jeopardise their chances," she says. She adds that it would be fine to accept a coffee offered by the employer, however, or drink one on a video interview. Dan Craddock, director at Hays, says employers shouldn't rely on "snap judgements". "It's important not to read too much into a single item a candidate brings to an interview. "Whether that's an iced coffee, a bottle of water or a notebook, employers are ultimately assessing the skills, experience and behaviours that will make someone successful in the role." Chris Mason, co-founder of Intelligent People - a specialist recruitment agency for the tech industry, says focusing on ice coffees alone "does seem to be an overreaction on the US recruiter's part". He advises candidates to "try to do everything possible to project the right image and attitude". He warns bringing snacks or specialist drinks may undermine the impression candidates will want to give - that they're "serious and focused on the interview". He says the main issue they see with some younger candidates is a lack of preparation, not being punctual, and not researching the role, organisation or interviewer.
