events.title: A Network-on-Chip (NoC) For Multi-Die Devices
events.summary: The semiconductor industry is rapidly transitioning from monolithic SoCs to chiplet-based architectures. At the same time, AI workloads are evolving beyond cloud inference into physical AI: systems that perceive, reason, and act in the real world. Autonomous vehicles, industrial robots, humanoid robots, drones, and intelligent manufacturing systems all require continuous, high-volume data flow between heterogeneous compute engines. However, these two trends expose a weakness in today’s die-to-die communication architectures. While coherent interconnect protocols have been highly successful for processor-centric systems, they are fundamentally mismatched to the traffic patterns generated by modern AI accelerators. As a result, a new approach is needed that involves transporting the native packetized traffic of the NoC directly across die boundaries using a stable, invariant interface. Physical AI changes the nature of on-chip communication Traditional processors are dominated by memory accesses, synchronization, and cache coherence. Physical AI systems are different. A modern automotive compute platform may simultaneously execute: Multiple camera processing pipelines Radar and lidar signal processing Sensor fusion AI perception networks Localization and mapping Path planning Functional safety monitoring Vehicle actuator control Rather than exchanging individual cache lines, these engines often exchange continuous streams of feature maps, tensors, point clouds, video frames, and intermediate inference results. These data streams often consist of hundreds of kilobytes, or even megabytes, moving between specialized accelerators at deterministic rates. The communication pattern resembles a high-performance dataflow network more than a coherent symmetric multi-processor system. As physical AI systems become more capable, the amount of accelerator-to-accelerator traffic continues to grow faster than CPU-to-memory traffic. Where coherent protocols excel Coherent die-to-die protocols remain the right solution for many applications and perform exceptionally well for: Coherent communication between processor dies in large SMP systems CPU memory accesses Synchronization Control-plane communication from CPUs to I/O management processors or accelerators These protocols were designed to maintain memory consistency while moving relatively small cache-line-sized transactions. For processor-centric workloads sharing memory, they are extremely effective. Why are they inefficient for AI data movement? Accelerator traffic follows very different patterns. Most coherent protocols divide communication into cache-line-sized transactions, typically 64 bytes each. Every cache line carries protocol overhead, including: Addresses Transaction identifiers Ordering information Response tracking Coherence metadata When transferring large tensors or feature maps, this overhead must be repeated thousands of times. For AI workloads, the actual payload accounts for only a portion of the transmitted bandwidth, with protocol overhead consuming an increasingly significant fraction of the available die-to-die bandwidth. Some coherent protocols have added optimizations to help improve the efficiency of non-coherent, bursty traffic. While useful, these mechanisms are limited in scope. For example, they span only a small number of beats and cannot fully ameliorate the overhead associated with very long streaming transfers of arbitrary data. As accelerator bandwidth increases into the terabytes-per-second range inside future automotive AI systems, repeatedly transmitting cache-line metadata becomes increasingly difficult to justify. Existing approaches Many non-coherent die-to-die approaches have been proposed, including: AMD/Xilinx AXI Chip2Chip, which is deployed in FPGA implementations. Open Chiplet Atlas (OCA) AXI over UCIe (AoU), a proposal from Tenstorrent/OCA. Various proprietary approaches that serialize AXI over high-speed serial interfaces. These approaches extend AXI interfaces across die boundaries and work well for connecting peripherals and control-oriented IP. However, they still operate at the transaction layer. Each NoC packet of each virtual channel must be converted into AXI transactions before crossing the die boundary, then reconstructed as NoC packets on the receiving side. As systems scale to dozens of AI engines across multiple chiplets, this repeated conversion adds unnecessary latency, buffering, and implementation complexity. Fig. 1: Multi-die interconnect in physical AI applications. Source: Arteris, Inc . Direct NoC-to-NoC communication A more natural architecture is to allow the NoC itself to span multiple dies. Instead of terminating the NoC at each chiplet boundary, native NoC packets are transported directly across the die-to-die interface. The remote die simply becomes another portion of the same logical network. This provides several important advantages: Streaming transfers remain packetized from producer to consumer without being repeatedly converted into cache-line transactions and AXI interfaces. Protocol overhead is amortized across long data streams rather than repeated for every cache line. Virtual channels enable multiple traffic classes, including control traffic, real-time sensor data, AI inference traffic, and bulk DMA transfers, to share the same physical die-to-die connection while maintaining quality of service (QoS). Existing NoC routing, arbitration, congestion management, and QoS mechanisms naturally extend across multiple dies. Multiple protocols can be transported over the same die-to-die interface: for example, AXI, APB, AHB or OCP. Most importantly, the die boundary ceases to be a protocol translation point. It simply becomes an additional hop in a single, multi-die network-on-chip. Why does this matter for automotive physical AI? Automotive AI places unique demands on interconnects. Unlike cloud AI systems, automotive platforms must satisfy strict latency, determinism, power, and functional safety requirements while operating within tight thermal limits. Centralized vehicle compute platforms will integrate multiple AI chiplets connected through advanced packaging technologies. Individual chiplets may specialize in: Vision processing Neural network inference Radar processing Lidar processing CPU clusters Safety and security islands Memory expansion Networking The largest traffic flows are often not between CPUs and memory but between accelerators themselves. For example: Camera processing → AI perception → Sensor fusion → Planning → Vehicle control Shared tensor movement between multiple neural-network accelerators These are fundamentally streaming dataflow applications. Transporting these streams using a native packetized NoC enables far more efficient bandwidth utilization, while reducing latency and buffering throughout the system. events.title: Managing 3D-IC Design And IP
events.summary: By Keith Felton and Todd Burkholder The trend towards multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration is here to stay. It promises faster innovation, more powerful and specialized devices, and greater design flexibility. However, realizing its potential hinges on our ability to manage the complexity that comes with it. However, with this newfound modularity comes a significant challenge: managing the vast and intricate web of data that defines these systems. This is where robust data management and meticulous data traceability become not just beneficial, but essential. Without data management, even the most brilliant multi-chiplet design can quickly become a tangled mess, leading to costly errors, delays, and a loss of confidence in the final product. In the first three articles of this series (published in the June , July and August editions of Semiconductor Engineering), we covered the first seven steps toward streamlining your 3D-IC design process. This article focuses on design data and design IP management, traceability, and revision control. This is a critical step for multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration, as there is so much design data and IP involved that using an incorrect version or missing an ECO can mean product failure. Data management can be broken down to four components that will help you streamline your 3D-IC design flow: Management of the many sources of design IP Design hierarchy with revision control and history tracking A centralized data and information hub Instant status tracking and analysis A plethora of IP In the world of multi-chiplet design, we often bring together various pieces of IP from different sources—from internal teams, external vendors, or even open-source initiatives. Each piece of design IP comes with its own set of design files, specifications, and usage guidelines. When you have multiple chiplets from different sources, potentially designed with different tools and at different times, the sheer volume and diversity of this data can be overwhelming. Without a well-defined data management strategy to manage these diverse sources, the risk of introducing defects is significantly higher. Innovator3D IC Data Management software supports robust data and design IP management to provide single moment-of-truth management of design IP data. It treats the design itself as a work-in-progress, applying a revision-controlled and access-rights managed process at every stage of design, all the way to tape out. Fig. 1: Innovator3D IC Data Management’s centralized cockpit. Managing design hierarchy Multi-chiplet designs inherently involve a complex hierarchy. Chiplets are integrated into a larger multi-chiplet heterogeneous assembly using interposers and substrates. Managing this hierarchy effectively, especially with the inevitable design iterations, requires a powerful revision control system. When you manage your design hierarchy with revision control and history tracking, you avoid errors. Revision control is like a time machine for your designs. It allows you to track every change, revert to previous versions, and allow different teams to work on separate features or bug fixes concurrently without interfering with each other. Once a team’s work is complete and verified, their changes can be merged back into the main design. Without this meticulous historical tracking, understanding how a design evolved, diagnosing issues, or even just knowing which version is currently “in play” becomes a monumental task. Errors can appear through miscommunication or accidental overwriting, leading to significant delays and increased costs. A well-managed design hierarchy with robust revision control is fundamental to preventing these types of errors. Centralized data and information hub In a distributed design environment, where different teams might be working on different chiplets across various locations, having a single, centralized hub for all design data is invaluable. This hub acts as the single source of truth, providing direct access to all relevant information for authorized personnel. When engineers can quickly access information they need, cycle times are dramatically reduced. This direct access speeds up design, verification, and debugging processes, leading to faster time-to-market. Instant status tracking and analysis Beyond just storing data, an effective data management system provides real-time visibility into a project’s status. This capability is crucial for efficient project management, especially in the complex landscape of multi-chiplet integration. Instant access to status tracking and analytical data empowers project managers and engineering leads to make informed decisions, proactively address issues, and ensure that the project stays on track. It transforms data from a passive record into an active tool for driving project success. By embracing robust data management practices, including diligent management of the design and its IP sources, meticulous revision control, centralized information hubs, and comprehensive status tracking for traceability, you establish a solid foundation for success. These “unseen architects” ensure that your multi-chiplet designs are not only functional and perform well, but also are reliable, maintainable, and auditable — allowing you to build the complex, interconnected systems of tomorrow with confidence and clarity. Burkholder began his career in marketing for high-technology and other industries in 1992 after earning a Bachelor of Science at Portland State University and a Master of Science degree from the University of Arizona. events.title: When AI Agents Cross Chip Design Silos
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Chip design is moving toward specialized AI agents working together. Orchestration, integration, and guardrails are becoming critical. Human engineers still play a central role in guiding and validating designs and processes. AI agents are becoming smarter, more capable, and increasingly optimized for specific tasks, creating new opportunities to use smaller language models instead of relying on large language models for every task. This shift has broad implications for the semiconductor industry, from the actual design and manufacturing of chips to how those chips function under different workloads. While LLMs can deploy swarms of agents for continuous reasoning and independent action, that’s overkill for most applications. But reducing the size of the model, and potentially the number or capability of the agents, adds its own challenges. One approach is to divide complex workflows among smaller language models and agents, while still retaining the compute capability needed to design, optimize, floor-plan, verify, and debug chips, and to identify anomalies and variations in manufacturing processes that might limit yield. This approach combines both human expertise with AI’s ability to crunch massive amounts of data. “In our early work on agents, which we created for each of our tools, we have questions and answers,” said Prith Banerjee, senior vice president of innovation at Synopsys . “We had an agent for this, and an agent for that. But in this world of multi-agent workflows, our customers are trying to design a chip. Maybe they’re having a problem with the PPA, and some engineers say they know exactly what changes are needed to lower the power. So they’ll do clock gating, but when you do clock gating, it increases the area. Then, someone who is the area expert will come in. This is exactly what happens in the real world, where multiple people come together and design a system with coordination. The human manager is coordinating the activities of the human agents in a multi-agent framework.” The next step is how to automate and combine more of those processes, and that requires more guardrails to limit what AI can do. “The model is drawing a boundary,” said Mo Faisal, CEO of Movellus . “It’s like, ‘Hey, you’re getting in the domain that I work in. Stay in your lane.’ We will specialize. A couple of [huge] companies will take the LLMs, but everybody else has to specialize. And AI, by the way, is not just LLMs. That’s the biggest use, but it’s not the definition of AI. AI intelligence can be used in many areas. People are building AI for chips, but there’s also AI for everything — accounting, lawyers, weather prediction, and all of those are different and unique workloads. But you don’t need to use LLMs for weather prediction. That’s inefficient.” The good and bad of specialization is that agents need to be configured and integrated into existing tools and workflows. Making all of that work seamlessly is hard work. It requires orchestration by other agents, or teams of agents, that have been trained to fit together these potentially overlapping steps. And it requires a whole different way of approaching the problem, where CPU-based orchestration may be as important, if not more important, than GPU-based multiply-accumulate operations. “We’ve gone to the aggregation level with ‘super agents,’ and we think their complexity and the amount of value they can deliver is as big or bigger than EDA tools,” said Matt Graham, senior group director of verification software product management at Cadence . “These are a new category of tools, and we’re starting to talk less about agents than skills that are dynamically assembled into agents. But the idea is that it’s all handled by a kind of orchestrating super-agent. And just like our customers have always arranged our tools into flows with their own custom scripting, they’re going to arrange our super agents and agentic workflows and solutions the way they need by writing their own scripts and putting them into a flow.” Those super agents (or lead agents, managing agents, or just agents — this is so new that naming conventions are constantly changing), as well as sub-agents that are managed by those super-agents, and they can be used in tandem or managed separately. “You can have sub-agents do different things, and then for other things we have a multi-agent solution,” said William Wang, CEO of ChipAgents . “We released a multi-agent solution to the industry in Q4 of last year, and it’s multi-agent coordination for things like debugging. If your SoC is so big, how are you going to optimize the performance? To do that, you need multiple agents with parallel access to different contexts to do the job. Similarly, with functional/formal verification, you can have multiple agents looking at different color groups to do the debugging and be able to optimize. Those are extremely critical.” The integration problem Chip design and manufacturing require repeatability and predictability, but many of the leading-edge chips are unique. This is particularly true for multi-die assemblies, which are often optimized for specific data types or applications, such as data centers, smartphones, and robotics. At the same time, whatever actions agents take need to be compatible with existing tools, flows, or processes, which must adapt to the rapid evolution of agentic AI. “Typically, customers will work within a platform, and that could be Cadence Virtuoso, Synopsys Custom Compiler, or Keysight Advanced Design system, and within that environment we guide them through an application-specific workflow,” said Niels Faché, senior vice president at Keysight EDA . “We have in-product documentation to explain all the different steps, setups, and possibilities of the tools. That’s all designed for human engineers to collaborate and work on complex products. With AI, that’s becoming a very different model where human engineers work with digital engineers or agents. So now we have to redesign our products. You’ve heard about MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, where we look at a product and ask, ‘How can we now modularize it, provide access to different capabilities with the proper APIs?’ All of that coding is typically done in Python, and that would then allow an agent to stitch together a code-based workflow. Our job is to make sure that our customers get this MCP functionality.” Making that approach work requires better-defined goals for agents to work both independently and in concert with other agents, and better training of the agents to achieve those goals. “If you want an agent to perform a certain task — it could be synthesizing a filter — you would say, ‘I&#

events.title: EDA’s Future Is Evidence-Driven Automation
events.summary: Key Takeaways : AI’s biggest EDA opportunity is workflow-level orchestration that coordinates tools, people, constraints, and domain knowledge across traditionally fragmented design stages, rather than merely improving individual tools. Trust requires evidence and semantic continuity. AI-generated recommendations or assertions must preserve design intent and remain independently verifiable through deterministic verification, formal proof, reproducibility, and audit trails. The emerging EDA model is human-guided, agentic automation. AI handles repetitive coordination, exploration, debugging, and handoffs, while engineers retain control over specifications and signoff. Established EDA engines provide the ground truth. AI is arriving in EDA at a time when engineers can no longer depend on brute-force scaling for performance and power improvements, and when the gaps created by disconnected point tools are becoming increasingly time-consuming to fill. As designs expand to tens of billions of transistors and incorporate chiplets in multi-die assemblies, the hardest problems increasingly sit between tools — preserving intent, managing interdependencies, and identifying potential failures before they reach tapeout. At advanced nodes, where design costs can reach hundreds of millions of dollars and a single respin can threaten an entire program, AI’s real value will depend on whether it can accelerate various steps in the design flow while organizing and interpreting the data needed to trust the results. The balance is between reliability and practicality. The global shortage of skilled engineers has not gone away. But it has made workflow automation more attractive, provided it can either improve the productivity of human engineers or achieve comparable results. “Every customer is saying, ‘Give me the ability to shrink my time to results by at least 2×,’” said Ankur Gupta, executive vice president and head of EDA IC software at Siemens EDA . “Demand is pushing EDA toward a new operating model built on faster engines, smarter execution, and trusted outcomes. Acceleration may come from GPUs, machine learning, or reinforcement learning, but the larger goal is to shorten design cycles without losing confidence in the result.” Efficiency also matters at the agent layer. Allowing any agent to call any tool may be flexible, but it can be expensive and inefficient if the underlying interfaces are poorly written. The goal is to do more of that integration work in advance so customers can either use a vendor’s agents or their own without paying unnecessary token and orchestration costs. The economics of AI are becoming increasingly important as engineers incorporate it at various places in the design process. “If I spend more money on tokens than a human would cost, then it doesn’t make sense,” said Thomas Andersen, vice president of the AI Excellence Group at Synopsys . “Agentic AI is useful only when it reduces the cost and complexity of production workflows. An agentic loop can perform sequences of tasks that an expert would otherwise handle manually, from automating repetitive steps to coordinating work across tools. Everybody wants to automate their workflows. They want agentic automation because that’s their way to productivity, to faster tape-out cycles, cutting costs, everything.” The hard part isn’t dropping a tool. It’s integrating agents into real customers’ design flows. Current challenges Semiconductor design is inherently a multi-tool process, spanning architecture, IP configuration, integration, verification, implementation, and sign-off. The challenge is not simply moving data from one tool to another, but preserving the design intent, assumptions, and engineering context behind that data. “At the system level, where connectivity, address maps, performance constraints, and security requirements must remain consistent across many IP blocks and, increasingly, across multiple dies, engineers often serve as the integration layer,” explained Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing at Arteris . That becomes increasingly difficult as systems grow in complexity. “The same architectural intent may be represented differently across integration, performance analysis, verification, and implementation environments,” Nightingale said. “If those representations diverge, the result can be additional verification cycles, manual rework, and late discovery of system-level issues. Better optimization between tools therefore needs to provide semantic continuity across the design flow, not simply file-format interoperability.” Still, AI’s real impact on EDA will be less about sign-off and more about streamlining the peripheral process and data-management work around the flow. “There’s as much value there now as in the core simulators and layout tools, and that’s where AI can help you get things done much faster,” said Chris Mueth, new opportunities business manager at Keysight EDA . Chip design is essentially a relay race involving dozens of specialized tools, including architectural exploration, RTL, lint, clock-domain crossing, formal, simulation, synthesis, place-and-route, timing and power sign-off, physical verification, equivalence checking, DFT, and post-silicon correlation. “Each was written by a different vendor, against a different data model, with different assumptions about what ‘done’ means,” said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise . “The relay is where most of the pain lives. As the Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective survey puts it, EDA is ‘inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy,’ and every artifact crosses tool, session, and organizational boundaries before signoff. Each transfer is a chance to lose information, silently reinterpret intent, or push a decision that was locally optimal in one tool into a globally suboptimal position downstream.” Darbari groups the core workflow challenges into a few recurring failure modes: No shared semantic model. Synthesis, P&R, and signoff are still optimized for local objectives because they cannot reliably see downstream consequences. Integrated platforms help within one vendor stack, but semantic gaps remain wide across vendors and between design and verification. Handoff loss between design and verification. RTL often carries intent that never makes it into machine-checkable form, forcing engineers to re-derive testbenches, assertions, coverage models, constraints, and waivers from ambiguous English. Silicon success data underscores the cost. First-time silicon success has fallen sharply, with most respins still traced to design errors. That is a workflow and intent-transfer problem, not simply a compute problem. Fragmented data formats and closed databases. events.title: AI-Driven Device Modeling For Next Generation Quantum Applications
events.summary: Key takeaways: Accelerate quantum system design by rapidly developing accurate device models for circuit-level simulation. Reduce manual model-tuning effort with Keysight ML Optimizer, enabling efficient, derivative-free extraction of advanced compact model parameters. Extend compact models to cryogenic temperatures using deep learning neural networks (NN) to learn unmodeled residual behavior from 4 K or below measurement data. Quantum computing is advancing rapidly from isolated research devices toward increasingly complex and scalable systems. This growth is driven by cloud deployments and breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, optimization, and simulations, pushing the market to a 41.8% CAGR from 2025 to 2030 [Source: https://www.marketsandmarkets.com] . But scaling a quantum processor is not only a challenge for the qubits, couplers or Josephson junctions themselves; it is also a challenge for the electronics that control, bias, and read out those devices sitting on a cryo-electronics wafer integrated alongside the qubit wafer. Much of the supporting electronics must operate at cryogenic temperatures, often only a few degrees above absolute zero. As more control and readout functionality moves closer to the quantum processor, the need for accurate models of semiconductor devices operating at these temperatures becomes increasingly important. The modeling challenge of moving from 300K to 4K A common challenge modeling engineers face is to develop accurate and computationally efficient device models when low temperature physics is either not fully understood, or available compact models are not yet standardized which is further exacerbated by lack of specialized measurement setup needed at cryogenic temperatures. Parameters such as threshold voltage, carrier transport, leakage, and transconductance also shift substantially. Additional low-temperature effects also become important, including dopant freeze-out and changes in carrier statistics and band structure below 10K. This creates a new challenge for device modeling and circuit design engineers: How do you develop accurate, simulation-ready device models at cryogenic temperatures without spending months manually tuning parameters or developing new physics-based equations from scratch? This matters because without accurate models, engineers cannot confidently simulate and optimize cryogenic control circuits, readout electronics, low-noise amplifiers, and other critical components of a quantum system. In this blog, we introduce a workflow that starts with extracting a high-quality baseline BSIM-BULK compact model using the Keysight ML Optimizer for room temperature (300K) data and then uses hybrid Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) to learn cryogenic behavior that model cannot capture as shown in Figure 1. Fig. 1: Flowchart shows the Hybrid ANN approach. Automatic extraction at 300 K The first step is to establish a high-quality model fit for room temperature measurement data. Most state-of-the-art compact models tend to be non-linear where multiple parameters interact strongly. Traditional optimizers such as Levenberg-Marquardt, Genetic algorithm etc. either get stuck in local minima or take too long to converge to a global solution and hence, lead to weeks of iterative tuning across numerous extraction steps. On the other hand, Keysight ML optimizer continuously learns and refines the parameter space while offering a derivative-free approach to simultaneously extract over 80 parameters in a single extraction step. Using Skywater 130nm IV & CV data at 300K for a PMOS device, we build a full global model extraction flow for BSIM-BULK compact model involving just 5 steps where each step involves extracting relevant parameters using ML optimizer. This extraction procedure establishes a physics-based BSIM-BULK model reference against which cryogenic behavior of this extracted model can be compared. Fig. 2: Final fitting of Id & derivatives for smallest and narrowest devices at 300K using BSIM-BULK v107.1 Cryogenic model extension at 4 K using IC-CAP ANN toolbox It would be ideal to extend an existing compact model to 4 K, but BSIM-BULK currently lacks the equation needed to model the physical effects at cryogenic temperatures in CMOS devices. Going through the development process for such a physical model can take significant research, time, and standardization efforts. This is precisely where ANNs can complement the compact model by learning the residual behavior that remains after the physics-based model has been evaluated at 4K, which is the fundamental concept behind the hybrid ANN modeling approach. On the other hand, a standalone full ANN must learn device physics, temperature scaling, non-linearities, bias dependence etc., from scratch which requires significantly more training data and time, making physics interpretation and extrapolation more difficult. A typical forward propagation ANN architecture used is shown in Fig. 3 below. Fig. 3: Input layer, Hidden layer and Output layer setup of the ANN residual. Hybrid ANN acts as an intelligent correction layer than a replacement for compact models, making modeling problems at hand substantially more manageable especially when measurement data is limited. Using the Keysight ANN toolbox in Device Modeling IC-CAP 2027, the neural network training process can be structured around the difference in drain currents between the measured 4K data and the baseline prediction by BSIM-BULK model extracted at 300K across all biases and geometries including derivatives. Forward propagation ANN consisting of 2 hidden layers which represent geometry/bias interaction more efficiently, with 18 neurons per layer across optimization iterations to achieve an error tolerance of 7.5e-4, is used to train ANNs against the current residuals from 4K measurement data and simulations, with final fitting results shown in Figure 4 below. Finally, the trained hybrid ANN equations are converted into Verilog-A format and implemented as a current source in conjunction with the 300K model. Fig. 4: Final fitting of Id & derivatives for smallest and narrowest devices at 4K. A new device modeling workflow for next generation quantum system design As demonstrated above, once a cryogenic model has been accurately extracted in a matter of minutes, it can quickly become a building block for circuit-level design and simulations. Engineers can then directly use cryogenic models in Verilog-A to investigate readout circuits, low-noise amplifiers, and control electronics, etc., for system-level quantum design. This approach has several added values: Less engineering time spent on parameter extraction and optimization. events.title: Autonomy Levels For Design Agents: L1 To L5 Explained
events.summary: Agentic AI plays an important role in chip and system design, but not every “ agentic ” capability has the same degree of autonomy. In practice, autonomy is not binary. It is a progression from AI that optimizes bounded engineering tasks to systems that understand natural language, reason through design problems, and orchestrate multi-step workflows, each representing a different degree of autonomy. That difference matters. When design teams compare autonomy, the useful question is not simply whether a system is “agentic.” It is what the system can decide, what scope it owns, how its work is validated, when it asks for help, and who remains accountable for fallback and final signoff. This blog explains the practical progression from L1 through L5 and why a level label alone tells you very little unless it is tied to engineering scope, decision rights, validation depth, and human responsibility. Why autonomy levels matter now As designs grow larger, more heterogeneous, and harder to verify, engineering teams face a familiar challenge: the amount of work keeps expanding faster than the available time. More engineers and more scripts can help, but they do not fully solve the problem when design exploration, verification closure, implementation convergence, and signoff all require faster iteration across increasingly connected workflows. This is where Cadence agentic AI strategy comes in. Cadence describes its agentic AI approach as super agents that orchestrate and implement complex, multi-step workflows while remaining grounded in Cadence’s AI-optimized, physics-based design and verification tools. That positioning is important because EDA autonomy is only useful when decisions can be checked against trusted computational models, design rules, electrical models, and engineering best practices. The levels below are therefore not a race from “manual” to “fully automatic.” They are a way to compare how things change as AI takes on more responsibility: the scope of work, the degree of decision ownership, the validation loop, and the point at which the engineer must intervene. Understanding progression toward autonomy Cadence Agentic AI transforms chip and system design with design agents . This changes the engineer’s role from manual task execution to outcome-driven oversight, increasing productivity and accelerating the delivery of higher-quality designs. In leading-edge deployments, autonomous workflows have reduced development cycles from weeks to days. The Cadence framework defines five increasing levels of autonomy. These levels distinguish different types of capability, but they should not be treated as mutually exclusive product categories. A more autonomous workflow can incorporate Optimization AI, conversational capabilities, complex reasoning, and specialized agents from the levels beneath it. Nor do higher levels make the earlier ones obsolete; higher-level agentic workflows depend on strong underlying agents, engineering engines, and optimization technologies. A workflow built from inadequate individual capabilities will not produce an adequate overall result. L1: Optimization AI At L1, AI improves a bounded engineering task without owning the broader workflow. The system can explore alternatives, learn from results, and optimize parameters to meet an objective defined by the engineer. The differentiator is scope. AI may run extensive experiments in the background, but the engineer still owns the design intent, constraints, success criteria, and tradeoffs. Cadence Cerebrus AI Studio is a relevant example of AI-driven optimization for SoC implementation, using agentic AI workflows, advanced analytics, and optimization techniques to accelerate design closure and improve productivity. L2: Natural language as the interface If Level 1 is about computational heavy lifting, Level 2 is about reducing the communication barrier between human intent and machine syntax. Natural language becomes a practical interface to engineering tools and knowledge, enabling engineers to ask questions, request help, generate or debug code, and navigate tool capabilities in a conversational way. At L2, AI owns the interaction layer, not the full engineering objective; a fluent interface can make a tool easier to use without giving it independent authority over a design task. L3: Complex reasoning L3 crosses an important threshold: the AI is no longer only optimizing parameters or translating natural language. It can reason through a bounded engineering problem, generate a proposed result, check that result through engineering tools or evaluators, and iterate based on feedback. The differentiator is the reasoning-and-validation loop. A general-purpose model may produce plausible output, but EDA reasoning becomes useful when it is connected to linters checking, formal engines, simulation tools, APIs, or other evaluators that can test a result and provide feedback for the next iteration. Here, mental models act as structured knowledge representations that capture design intent, hierarchy, relationships, specifications, and historical context. At this level, that context helps agents reason about a bounded task with more discipline than a prompt-only interaction could. The engineer still defines the problem, reviews consequential conclusions, and can redirect or reject the result. L3 gives the AI more responsibility for reasoning, but not unrestricted ownership of the design objective. L4: Agentic workflows At L4, autonomy expands from a bounded reasoning task to a connected engineering workflow. Specialized agents coordinate planning, execution, validation, optimization, and iteration across multiple steps. The differentiator is orchestration. Cadence AI Super Agents coordinate specialized agents across domains and tools. Cadence describes ChipStack , ViraStack , InnoStack , and AuraStack as applying agentic AI across front-end design and verification, analog design, digital implementation and signoff, PCB, and advanced packaging workflows. The engineer defines the goal, constraints, and acceptance criteria, while the system coordinates the path forward. What makes L4 different from L3 is not simply “more AI.” It is the coordination of multiple skills, tools, and agents toward a broader engineering outcome. As the scope expands, governance becomes more important because one agent’s output may affect later steps in the flow. Shared design context, tool-based validation, monitoring, and exception handling help keep orchestration anchored in engineering reality. L5: Full autonomy within a defined engineering scope L5 represents autonomous execution within a defined engineering scope. Cadence ChipStack AI Super Agent operates at Level 5 autonomy for complex chip design and verification workflows, while engineers can inspect, guide, and collaborate as needed. events.title: 3D Chips Push EDA Into New Territory
events.summary: Key Takeaways : EDA tools are helping design 3D-ICs and multi-die systems by co-optimizing across domains and speeding up design exploration. Customers face several pain points, including vendor interoperability, dynamic floor-planning, IR analysis, and STA analysis. Agentic AI adds an extra layer on existing tools and serves as the foundation for new startup solutions. As demand for AI power and performance grows, chip designs increasingly involve 3D stacking, chiplets, and heterogeneous integration within a single package. In a virtuous cycle, EDA tool vendors are leveraging advanced chips to simulate multi-physics challenges in a single tool instead of running individual solvers. Agentic AI is adding another layer of analysis to enable faster design exploration and automate various tasks. However, a few speed bumps remain due to the rapid progression of chip technology. One challenge is that HPC/AI chip design must be considered across compute, memory, interconnect, power, and thermal constraints. “Today, nearly every AI accelerator has a process threshold where the hardest problems no longer live inside the chip. They live at the system boundaries,” said Artour Levin, vice president of AI silicon engineering at Microsoft.[1] “A standalone chip is not very beneficial for AI because very few things can be run on a single chip. You really need to look at the system level, and if you look at the history of EDA tools when they started, 30 or 40 years ago, it’s natural that EDA tools were designed to design chips, not a system.” The chip-to-system threshold is where customers are facing challenges. “The design toolchain grew up around clean abstraction boundaries — cell, block, chip — with physics handled as episodic, domain-by-domain validation at the end,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO and co-founder of Vinci . “That operating model worked when the hardest problems stayed inside those boundaries. It breaks when heat, stress, and electrical behavior move across the entire physical stack, because the physics insight arrives after the decisions that needed it have already been made. Hardware teams don’t need physics after the design is done changing. They need physics while the design is still moving.” That requires new approaches, not a faster version of the old workflow. “It’s deterministic, solver-accurate physics that’s continuously available across chip, package, board, and system — treating physics as infrastructure rather than a late-stage checkpoint,” said Kabaria. “In hardware, plausible isn’t enough. Outputs have to be measurable, deterministic, and accurate enough to support real design decisions, which is why solver-grounded results and run-to-run reproducibility matter as much as speed.” The central question is whether to augment existing EDA tools that have been fine-tuned and proven over many years, or create new tools because AI/HPC chip designs are so different from the monolithic chips of days gone by. “There are decades of embedded knowledge for good reason, and a lot of long-held beliefs that work in single isolation, but maybe not when you go cross-domain,” said Henry Sheng, executive director of R&D at Synopsys .[2] “This has to be reflected within the tooling itself. How do you manage not to try to boil the ocean? If you try to reinvent everything, you won’t do it. You have to reinvent how you put things together to maintain coherency, so you don’t have different data representations and terminologies for the same thing across domains. Then, how do you bring all that into a cohesive tool?” Heterogeneity puts more pressure on floor-planning challenges, in particular. “It becomes much harder, and that’s one of the conversations that people are having,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA . “Can we do the floor planning upfront? Can we make sure we all agree that this is the budget that you get for loss here, and this is the budget I get for signal path, and this is the way we are going to supply power to this complex 3D environment? That conversation starts happening up front, and it leaves very little room for negotiation later.” And while the big money says to use 3D design for AI chips, it can be applicable anywhere, Kamdar added. Maybe in the future, 3D and heterogeneous design will be out of the box, but that’s not the reality now. “Because the manufacturing and packaging technology is evolving fast, there’s still different solutions out there,” said Michal Siwinski, executive vice president, chief product and marketing officer at Arteris . “You can do it this way. You can do it that way. It’s not yet one size fits all. Because of that, people want some differentiation. But is the technology 80% there? Is it 90% there, where anybody who actually wants to do it can do it? Yeah, I think so.” Specific customer challenges Customers designing 3D-ICs and multi-die assemblies for AI/HPC chips are using existing EDA tools, but they want improvements in some areas. One challenge is interoperability across established vendors and startups. “If you want to put out compelling products in the industry, EDA tools should be very interoperable,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&D for advanced packaging technology and manufacturing at Intel . [3]. “I happened to look at a design last week. Just by experience, I said, ‘I don’t see enough density in some of these layers. Copper density is critical for warpage.’ I was very concerned that this might be a technical glitch. I reached out to my mechanical analysis person. I said, ‘Here you go. I think it is one of the other industry formats, but it doesn’t matter. We need to let the design team know that they might have to co-optimize the design, so they don’t get into issues later.’ It took 10 days for the analysis and a response. People looked at the design. They saw it wasn’t complete. It didn’t have some properties. Maybe it wasn’t completely routed. Then I pulled in a design engineer. They finished up with AI. They wrote some scripts, routed it, but then the extraction didn’t happen in a very prominent industry analysis capability. What I got was three pictures. One is yellow. One is red, and who knows what the other color is. And if I am a customer, as a design person, I look at it and don’t know what I need to do to the design. It makes no sense. events.title: US will make up to $7 billion in loans to help Trump ally Milei tap Argentina’s oil and minerals
events.summary: The Trump administration wants to put billions of dollars into Argentina’s energy and mining industries BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- The Trump administration said Wednesday it would set aside $7 billion for loans to support energy, mining and infrastructure projects in Argentina, its latest move to secure energy and critical minerals closer to home and back the South American country's libertarian president. The U.S. Export-Import Bank, a federal agency, would make up to $7 billion available through 2027 for projects in Argentina, the State Department said, helping companies in the country obtain loans to buy American equipment and hire U.S. firms to expand the country’s railways, pipelines, ports and power networks. The deal advances U.S. President Donald Trump’s effort to reduce reliance on China’s mineral processing industry , as well as bolstering his ally President Javier Milei , who is betting on oil, gas and mineral exports to transform Argentina’s economy and ease the chronic dollar shortages that have fueled repeated economic crises. “Working together, the United States and Argentina seek to continue to build on our robust relationship through increased U.S. investment, close security cooperation and aligned values," the State Department said in a statement. The relationship has already paid dividends for Milei's Argentina: Last year, Washington backed a $20 billion International Monetary Fund bailout for Argentina and extended a separate $20 billion currency-swap line to stabilize the Argentine peso. The countries also signed a free trade pact earlier this year. 5th grade teacher, student die during field trip to nature reserve Doctor stabbed to death while sleeping; wife wounded, kids escape unharmed Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber dies at 27 On the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said on Wednesday that the agreement aims to connect Argentina’s lithium- and copper-rich northwest and sprawling Vaca Muerta shale fields to the country’s ports, making it easier to ship minerals, oil and gas to the U.S. and other markets. Inadequate transport and energy infrastructure has long hampered development of Argentina’s remote deposits. The country's history of protectionist trade policies, currency controls and sovereign debt defaults has also discouraged foreign investment. Milei, a fierce believer in free markets, has moved to open Argentina's economy, scrapping import restrictions and offering tax breaks to attract investors. That has led to a surge in cheap imports, squeezing labor-intensive industries like manufacturing and retail already struggling under Milei's spending cuts and tight monetary policy. Booming oil production and mining exports have become an economic lifeline. The country has vast deposits of lithium and copper , minerals that are necessary for the global shift toward green energy. events.title: US increases pressure on Sudan
events.summary: The News The US State Department declared this week that neither of Sudan’s two warring factions is fit to govern, sharpening Washington’s pressure campaign as its push for a ceasefire stalls. “Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan — they rule through force of arms alone,” the State Department said in a statement Tuesday, vowing to raise the cost of fighting “on all belligerents and the networks which fuel the conflict.” The statement comes after more than a year of US efforts, led by President Donald Trump’s Africa adviser Massad Boulos, to secure a temporary ceasefire in Sudan’s three-year-old war, in which both sides have been accused of widespread abuses against civilians. The RSF has signaled it would accept a ceasefire, while the SAF — which has gained ground over the last year — has rejected a blanket truce. Washington responded by imposing “punitive measures” on the army in recent months, said Cameron Hudson, a veteran US-Africa affairs analyst and a former White House official under US President George W. Bush, including by imposing sanctions over the alleged use of chemical weapons and pushing to extend a UN arms embargo from RSF-controlled Darfur to all of Sudan. This week, the US reportedly restricted a visa for SAF leader Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan ahead of a planned appearance at the UN General Assembly. “What the US has been doing is ratcheting up pressure very steadily on the army with the assumption that it could get the pressure high and severe enough that the army would relent and sign a deal,” said Hudson. “The United States is committed to ending the horrific conflict in Sudan,” a State Department spokesperson told Semafor. “We are working with our partners to encourage the parties to agree to the humanitarian truce and guarantee humanitarian access, and to also ensure external military or financial support to the warring parties is cut off.” Know More Experts question whether the Trump administration’s strategy will work. EJ Hogendoorn, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former senior adviser to the US special envoy for Sudan, said that “the United States is expending a ton of political capital just to send a signal.” He warned that “temporary ceasefires tend to stay temporary,” pointing to dozens of past Sudanese truces that held only long enough for the combatants to regroup. The State Department’s declaration could also make diplomacy harder, Hudson argued. “The question that the Sudanese are asking themselves right now is how you engage in diplomacy with someone who you have now said very explicitly has no legitimacy to sit on the other side of the table from you,” he said. Boulos, speaking at Semafor’s The Next 3 Billion event Tuesday, stressed that Washington opposes any attempt to divide Sudan. “We are totally against any parallel governments,” he said. Asked whether the US still recognizes Sudan’s army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council, Boulos demurred: “There’s a de facto government that we deal with. It doesn’t mean that you officially recognize [it].” Step Back Washington’s hardline approach is also creating distance between the US and its regional allies seeking to end the war. After the State Department’s declaration on Tuesday, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan, and Türkiye issued a joint statement affirming their support for Sudan’s “sovereignty, unity, independence and territorial integrity.” It stressed the importance of preserving Sudan’s “legitimate national institutions” and rejecting “parallel entities.” “What this episode demonstrates is how isolated the United States has made itself,” Hudson said. The US is “moving in a very different direction from the rest of the countries that are engaging in diplomacy on Sudan.” The break could be particularly significant with Saudi Arabia. Trump agreed to help end the war after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked him to get involved , but the two countries’ approaches have increasingly diverged, particularly as Riyadh grows closer to the SAF, Hogendoorn said. “Because the SAF is resisting this ceasefire — and the US is obviously upset about that — that is driving a bit of difference between what the Saudis would like to see happen and what the administration is trying to achieve,” he said. Notable Sudan sought to counter the State Department’s comments , saying that it “upholds its national sovereignty,” Reuters reported . The UN Security Council will revisit expanding the arms embargo in mid-October , after extending the Darfur-only measure for a month amid resistance from China, Russia, and others.

events.title: Senators move to force AI companies to disclose more
events.summary: The push to regulate AI is intensifying in Washington, as a bipartisan group of senators rolls out an AI transparency bill on Thursday. According to details shared first with Semafor, the measure from Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., Katie Britt, R-Ala., Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, and James Lankford, R-Okla., would tap the Federal Trade Commission to enforce disclosure requirements for certain AI companies. They would be required to share information about how AI models work and the safeguards companies have in place to shield against misuse. “Americans deserve to know what [AI companies] are actually doing to place safety guardrails on large AI models,” Coons said in a statement. This bill is modestly focused on awareness about how AI works; other members of Congress have targeted more ambitious proposals, like all-out bans on “superintelligence” and economic plans for a new AI-enabled economy.

events.title: Some Republicans push to prioritize Husted data center bill
events.summary: The News Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, wants the Senate to stay in session until the body votes on his endangered colleague’s signature bill. Moreno told Semafor he believes the Senate should stay in until there’s a roll call vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, data center-focused energy legislation from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., blocked the bill last week. “Absolutely, 100%, they all hide behind Martin now, like it’s one Democrat. We need to put them on the record,” Moreno said. Republican senators have discussed the idea but made no final decision. “I have heard a lot of support from my colleagues about getting it done,” Husted told Semafor. “I hope we give [Democrats] another chance to get it right.” The Senate is scheduled to be in next week, but may cut the session short so lawmakers can hit the campaign trail. Know More It’s crunch time for the Senate schedule, and some Republicans would prefer the Senate break for the midterms and allow Republicans locked in difficult reelection battles to campaign. But for Husted, getting his bill done might be just as valuable as a week of campaigning. Rising public opposition to data centers, driven in part by their costs, has put pressure on lawmakers in Washington to come up with a solution. “Voters overwhelmingly support the idea of data centers paying their own way, so that they don’t run the risk of having to pay higher electricity prices as a result,” Husted said. “It could be the law of the land, and it could prove to Americans that we heard them, that we did something about it.” Heinrich blocked Husted’s bill and instead offered his own GRID Savings Act, which would require data centers to pay for power grid connections rather than making it voluntary. Other Democrats have criticized Husted’s bill as lacking teeth: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the measure, which passed the House overwhelmingly, a “fraud.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune acknowledged a “significant level of interest” in passing the bill. As he left the Capitol on Wednesday evening, his guidance for the Senate schedule was simply: “Don’t make any plans yet.”

events.title: Xi's visit met with Republican criticism
events.summary: Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s arrival in Washington — and the fanfare surrounding his visit — is running into criticism by some Republicans who are concerned about the optics. One person close to the White House told Semafor that rolling out the red carpet for Xi is “weird if POTUS lavishes a bunch of praise while simultaneously [saying] China is our biggest adversary.” Republicans seem to agree: Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker delivered a floor speech insinuating Trump should not be hosting Xi while four of his colleagues penned a letter reiterating concerns over Taiwan. The White House is brushing off the criticism, with spokeswoman Anna Kelly noting that Trump “is reciprocating” Xi’s “hospitality” after Trump visited China over the summer. “The president will forge relationships with anyone in order to advance our national interests and make good deals for the American people,” she added. The two countries have already agreed to extend a trade truce until next year, according to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Some Republicans have defended Trump for hosting the Chinese leader. “As somebody who represents an [agriculture] state, we need the market,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Wednesday. “We need to trade with them. So I think you want to figure out how to deal with the more controversial parts of the relationship, but there’s value in talking it out.” — Shelby Talcott and Eleanor Mueller

events.title: OpenAI agents breached Australian portal, attempted other hacks in routine data collection.
events.summary: OpenAI's autonomous agents breached an Australian Medicare portal and probed other public data sites in May and June after being stymied in routine data-collection efforts. Why it matters : The new incidents, which were revealed by security researchers and Australian officials Wednesday, indicate that the scope of rogue AI activity may be greater than what's been publicly acknowledged. The agents took those steps while engaged in ordinary data retrieval tasks, according to researchers, a distinction from other hacks by systems programmed specifically for cybersecurity work. The revelation is likely to raise fresh questions about OpenAI's internal controls and safeguards. Driving the news : Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI model breached the country's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service in June and accessed non-public files . The agents aren't believed to have accessed personal information, according to Albanese and OpenAI. This was part of a pattern of behavior that occurred in May and June, wherein the OpenAI agents sought to bypass data collection restrictions for several websites using a novel security technique. The models also attempted to hack a University of New Mexico website and a domain from Data USA, which aggregates and organizes government data, according to a report by AI safety firm Transluce. "Overall, the evidence is consistent with, but does not prove, that the agents may have learned this behavior over one or more training runs," according to the Transluce report. Catch-up quick : OpenAI has faced intense scrutiny after a swarm of its agents hacked AI platform Hugging Face in July to cheat on a cyber test. OpenAI last week disclosed six new incidents in which its models behaved in unexpected ways, and the company has since proposed a new framework for publicly reporting similar misbehavior in the future. CEO Sam Altman and other top AI executives, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Google's Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk, all said they would support a slowdown in frontier AI development after that and a spate of other similar incidents came to light . Reality check : Some cybersecurity pros and tech execs have said the problem has less to do with AI systems run amok and more to do with AI companies failing to proceed with sufficient caution. "Companies ought to ship safe products," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an interview with journalist Ezra Klein that was released Wednesday. "If your product is not ready to ship, don't ship the product." Zoom in : An OpenAI spokesman said the company discovered several instances involving Australian websites in which its models "took actions we did not intend" as it continues an investigation into "misaligned model activity." Albanese criticized how OpenAI disclosed the findings to Australia and said he expressed "extreme concern" to Altman when he spoke to him Wednesday. What's next : Australia is launching a multi-agency cyber task force to investigate the incident, consider legislative changes and whether it's necessary to refer the matter to federal police.
